USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current tariff posture and press forward in the active negotiation toward a final, enforceable deal rather than escalating. The talks are at their most advanced point yet — enforcement is 'pretty much agreed' and a US delegation heads to Beijing April 30 with Liu He to Washington May 8 — so the lever that delivers maximum US value is closing the deal, not raising the stakes. Keep the threatened List 3 hike from 10% to 25% in reserve as leverage, and do not tip the negotiation into a breakdown while the growth data is already soft.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests here is modest and tilt-negative: the US started this dispute, holds the stronger hand, and China is making concessionary progress on enforcement offices and purchases (April 10 Mnuchin; timeline entry 2019-04-03 intensive Washington talks with progress on enforcement text). That is the -0.5 'opportunity' anchor — leverage to restructure the trade relationship on US terms and a domestic political boost — though not -1.0 because escalating carries genuine second-order risk: US industrial production is sliding (102.3 in April vs 104.1 in Nov, -1.7%) and the 10Y/2Y spread has compressed toward ~21bp (10Y 2.53% vs 2Y 2.32%), a near-inversion growth warning that means pushing into a tariff war breakdown could feed recession risk. On the action axis, escalation now (raising/expanding the $250B tariff base to 25%) would risk scuttling an advanced negotiation and amplifying that growth anxiety, while full concession is premature — no final deal, enforcement specifics unresolved, and giving away leverage now forfeits the structural reforms and purchase commitments still at stake. The disciplined move is negotiate/hold at ~0.0: continue talks, hold tariffs as leverage, and only convert them on a signed, enforceable agreement.
key_factors: US holds leverage with ~$250B of Chinese imports already tariffed; talks at most advanced stage (enforcement 'pretty much agreed' Apr 10; Beijing delegation Apr 30)
US industrial production sliding to 102.3 (-1.7% since Nov) and 10Y/2Y spread compressed to ~21bp near-inversion — cap how hard the US can push without growth blowback
US exports to China rebounded to ~$10.6B in March while the goods deficit stays wide (-$74.4B) — dispute has not yet healed the trade imbalance
Escalating the List 3 hike to 25% risks breaking an advanced negotiation; conceding now forfeits leverage before an enforceable deal exists

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue to engage constructively in the ongoing US-China negotiations without new concessions or escalation, pressing to hold the tariff line (Lists 1-3 at current 10-25% levels, List 3 hike suspended) and work toward removing the Section 301 tariffs as the talks approach a possible summit deal. Do not retaliate or raise our own barriers now, because our economy is already showing strain and escalation would only deepen the slowdown and jeopardize the de-escalation path that is currently open.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is material but short of existential: industrial output growth hit a 17-year low and February factory output contracted for the first time since January 2009, with December exports falling the most in two years and imports slumping (Reuters Mar 2019; Bloomberg/Guardian), while the tariff regime covers ~$250B of our exports to the US at 10-25%. Firm-level targeting of Huawei and the Meng Wanzhou case remain a live national-security front (Politico). That warrants a threat_score of +0.45, between the 'neutral' and 'high' anchors. However, the dispute is in an active de-escalation phase: the List 3 hike to 25% has been repeatedly deferred (Feb 24, Mar 1), and April 3 intensive Washington talks report 'major headway' with a deal possibly near and a possible Trump-Xi summit (VOA Apr 4). Because our real economy is already ailing, escalation would be self-harming, so the correct action is to negotiate — keep engaging, keep the tariff suspension, and avoid new commitments or retaliation — rather than to escalate or to capitulate prematurely on structural concessions.
key_factors: China industrial output at 17-year low; Feb 2019 factory output contracted first time since Jan 2009
December 2018 exports fell most in two years; early-2019 imports slumping
~$250B of Chinese exports under US Section 301 tariffs (Lists 1-3), List 3 hike to 25% suspended
Huawei/Meng Wanzhou firm-level targeting and Canadian detentions as parallel front
April 2019 Washington talks reporting headway; possible Trump-Xi summit; ongoing de-escalation path
